questions.prompt: Why does this playbook deliberately delay remediation, unlike most others in this level?
options: Because remediation tooling is slow to deploy
Because acting before scoping destroys visibility, tips off the attacker, and may still miss non-Kerberos persistence
Because domain controllers cannot be modified during business hours
Because legal approval is always required first
questions.explanation: Premature krbtgt resets and credential rotation remove your ability to observe the attacker while leaving other persistence intact. Scoping first enables a single coordinated remediation.

questions.prompt: What is the stated exception to scoping before remediating?
options: Active, ongoing damage -- data actively leaving or systems actively being destroyed -- where containment wins, but the call is made explicitly
When the attacker is known to be external
When the domain has fewer than five domain controllers
questions.explanation: Ongoing destruction or exfiltration justifies immediate containment, but the playbook stresses making that tradeoff deliberately rather than defaulting into it.

questions.prompt: Why must certificate revocation be part of the coordinated remediation event?
options: Certificates are stored alongside password hashes
Certificates survive password resets and the krbtgt double reset entirely, remaining valid until expiry or revocation
Revocation is required before any password reset can succeed
Certificates automatically expire during a krbtgt reset
questions.explanation: Certificate validity is independent of credentials, so an attacker holding one retains authentication capability through every credential rotation unless the certificate is revoked.

questions.prompt: What makes the rebuild-versus-remediate decision answerable?
options: A fixed threshold of compromised accounts
Scope -- an organization that knows exactly what the attacker touched can argue for remediation; one that doesn't is choosing between rebuilding and hoping
The number of domain controllers in the forest
Whether the attacker used malware or living-off-the-land techniques
questions.explanation: There is no clean technical threshold. What makes the risk decision defensible is confidence in scope, which is exactly what the scoping phase produces.
